# ecomp — the Amiga E compiler for the browser

![CI](https://github.com/gin0115/Amiga-E-Compiler-WebBased/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)
![License: GPL-3.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-GPL--3.0-blue)

> The Amiga E language and its v40 module set are the work of
> **[Wouter van Oortmerssen](https://strlen.com/)**, who has kindly granted
> permission to use the E libraries in this project
> (from [Aminet dev/e/amigae33a](https://aminet.net/package/dev/e/amigae33a)).
> Thank you, Wouter! Every binary this compiler produces carries that
> credit embedded in it.

A from-scratch compiler for the **Amiga E** programming language
(E v3.3a, 1997), written in zero-dependency JavaScript. It compiles E
source to genuine AmigaOS M68K hunk executables and bootable ADF floppy
images — usable as a node CLI or embedded as a pure ES-module library
(it runs in the browser too).

Faithfulness is the core value: behaviour is validated against the
**original 1997 compiler** by a differential test suite (115 programs,
byte-identical output), and ecomp's binary `.m` modules are accepted by
real `ec` itself.

---

## Quick start: the CLI

```sh
node tools/ecc.js --source=hello.e --out=hello
node tools/ecc.js --source=hello.e --adf=hello.adf   # bootable floppy too
```

```
options:
  --out=FILE        output path (default: source without .e)
  -o FILE           same as --out
  --adf=FILE.adf    also write a bootable 880K floppy image that runs
                    the program at boot (mount as DF0: in any emulator)
  --moduledir=DIR   extra directory to search for binary .m modules
                    (repeatable; like ec's EMODULES: assign)
  --warn            print semantic warnings
  --quiet           suppress informational output
  --version, --help
```

A source that declares `OPT MODULE` produces a **binary `.m` interface
module** instead of an executable (and yes, the original Amiga compiler
can import the result).

> **Note:** this repository is the **compiler only** (CLI + embeddable
> JS library). A browser IDE that runs the output on an emulated Amiga
> consumes this as a package and is published separately.

## Using ecomp in your own projects

ecomp is fully self-contained: **no Kickstart ROM, no Workbench disk, no
emulator and no npm packages are needed to compile.** Those images are
only used by the browser IDE to *run* your program on the embedded
emulated Amiga afterwards. The compiler output is a standard AmigaOS
executable you can take to any real Amiga or emulator you like.

**Get it** (any of):

```sh
git clone https://github.com/gin0115/Amiga-E-Compiler-WebBased.git ecomp
# or download a release / the ZIP from GitHub and unpack it anywhere
```

**Compile from your own project directory** — call the CLI by its path,
nothing needs installing:

```sh
cd ~/my-amiga-game
node ~/tools/ecomp/tools/ecc.js --source=game.e --out=game --adf=game.adf
```

`game` is a ready AmigaOS executable; `game.adf` is a bootable floppy that
runs it. Your `MODULE '*mymodule'` files resolve from your project
directory; OS modules (`'dos/dos'`, `'intuition/intuition'`, …) come from
ecomp's bundled `modules/` automatically.

**Use it as a JavaScript library** (node or browser, pure ES modules):

```js
import { parse }          from './ecomp/src/parser.js';
import { analyze }        from './ecomp/src/sem.js';
import { compileProgram } from './ecomp/src/codegen.js';
import { bootableAdf }    from './ecomp/src/adf.js';

const { program, errors } = parse(eSourceText, 'game.e');
const sem = analyze(program /*, { resolveModule } for MODULE imports */);
const { bin } = compileProgram(program, sem);   // Uint8Array: AmigaOS hunk exe
const adf = bootableAdf(bin);                   // Uint8Array: bootable floppy
```

The minimal file set for compiling is `src/` + `tools/` + `modules/`.
Everything else (the IDE, tests, emulator wiring) is optional.

| You want to… | You need |
|---|---|
| compile E → Amiga executables/ADFs | just these files + node ≥16 |
| run the output | any Amiga emulator (or real hardware) |
| watch it run in a browser | the separately published IDE package |

## Multi-file projects

ecomp follows real E's model — you always compile **one main source**, and
it pulls its modules in via `MODULE` statements:

```e
MODULE '*helper'       -> the * means: sibling file in the same directory
PROC main()
  greet('Amiga')
ENDPROC
```

```e
-> helper.e
OPT MODULE
EXPORT PROC greet(who)
  WriteF('hello, \s!\n', who)
ENDPROC
```

```sh
node tools/ecc.js --source=main.e    # helper resolves automatically
```

Resolution order for `MODULE 'name'` / `MODULE '*name'`:

1. a sibling `name.m` binary interface module
2. a sibling `name.e` source, compiled into your program
3. `--moduledir=DIR` directories (binary `.m`)
4. the bundled v40 OS module set (`modules/` — `'dos/dos'`,
   `'intuition/intuition'`, `'exec/lists'`, …)

The exec/dos/intuition/graphics library calls are preloaded implicitly,
exactly like real E — `OpenWindow()`, `ReadArgs()`, `MODE_NEWFILE` and
friends just work without any `MODULE` statement.

## What's implemented

Everything in the E v3.3a manual, including the famous corners:

- no operator precedence (`1+2*3` really is 9), 16-bit runtime `*`/`/`
  with ec's exact strength reductions, full-32-bit constant folding
- E-strings & E-lists with their length headers, `StrCopy`/`StringF`/…
- `OBJECT`s, inheritance, methods with `self`, constructors `NEW b.init()`,
  destructors via `END`, `SIZEOF`
- exceptions: `HANDLE`/`EXCEPT`/`EXCEPT DO` (a finally!), `Raise`, `Throw`
- quoted expressions `` `x*x ``, `Eval`, `MapList`/`ForAll`/`Exists`/`SelectList`
- LISP cells `<a|b>`, `Car`/`Cdr`/`Cons`, unification `exp <=> [1,x,y]`
- IEEE floats with the `!` operator (mathieeesingbas, like the real thing)
- inline M68K assembly with E variable access (ch_15)
- windows, screens, graphics and events: `OpenW`/`OpenS`, `Line`/`Box`/
  `Plot`/`TextF` on `stdrast`, `WaitIMessage`, `Mouse`
- the heap: `NEW`, `New()`, `String()`, `Dispose`, `Link`/`Next` chains,
  auto-free at exit
- 100+ builtins, the dos/exec call surface, `CleanUp`, `CtrlC`, `Rnd`…

## E-VO support (modern Amiga E) — opt-in

Beyond classic EC v3.3a, ecomp has an **optional E-VO extension** (Darren
Coles' modern Amiga E), enabled with an `evo` flag and contained entirely in
`src/evo/`. With the flag off (default) ecomp is faithful EC v3.3a; with it on
it accepts modern E as a strict superset — `//` comments, `<<`/`>>`, `NOT`/`~`,
compound assignment, `ANDALSO`/`ORELSE`, `IFN`/`WHILEN`/`ELSEWHILE`/`ALWAYS`/…,
ternary `?:`, swap `:=:`, `==` quick-compare, multi-dim arrays, `UNION`,
`NEW objtype.ctor()`, `TRY`/`CATCH`, `BYTE`/`WORD` types, `PSIZEOF`/`ARRAYSIZE`/
`OFFSETOF`, and the E-VO standard library (List/String/Astr/Mem families).

Validated against the real **E-VO compiler** (assembled from `E-VO.S` and run
under vamos as a third oracle): E-VO's own 741-test `unittests.e`, compiled by
ecomp in evo mode, runs to completion with **732 pass / 9 fail** vs EVO's own
**731 / 10** (the 9 are vamos-environment quirks EVO also fails). Native EC mode
is byte-identical with the flag on or off (115/115 differential still green).

See **[docs/evo-support.md](docs/evo-support.md)** for the full feature list,
the `src/evo/` architecture, and the three-compiler validation.

## Linking precompiled binary modules (EasyGUI, afc/*, oomodules/*, …)

ecomp doesn't just read a module's *interface* — it **links the actual 68K
code** out of the shipped binary `.m` files into your executable, the same
way the original `ec` does. Importing `tools/EasyGUI`, `afc/Parser`,
`oomodules/*` etc. pulls their compiled procedures straight in, no source
required. This is a small linker on top of the code generator:

- **Code + relocations** — each module's `CODE` blob is appended and its
  `RELOC`s applied (internal pointers rebased into `HUNK_RELOC32`; the
  placeholder `jsr abs.l` ifunc sites patched to `bsr.l` into the runtime).
- **The E runtime intrinsics** the modules call (`WriteF`, `String`, `Mod`,
  `RealF`, `SetColour`, …) are emitted as thunks ported **1-for-1** from
  the original `ec68kifuncs` source and **run-verified byte-identical to
  `ec`** under emulation (`tools/ifunc-verify.js`, 29/29).
- **The ABI matches `ec`.** Precompiled modules bake in `ec`'s fixed
  negative-`A4` offsets for the standard runtime globals (`dosbase` at
  `-44`, `stdout` at `-8`, …), so ecomp lays out `A4` to match — a module
  calling `dos.ReadArgs` finds its base exactly where `ec` put it.
- **OOP across the boundary** — classes from binary modules dispatch through
  their runtime vtable (the per-class "descriptor" the module builds itself):
  `NEW obj.class()` builds the descriptor, allocates, and calls the
  constructor; `obj.method()` dispatches via the slot; `END obj` runs the
  destructor and frees. Reverse-engineered from real `ec` output and written
  up in `docs/oop-dispatch.md`.

148 of the 149 shipped binary code modules link; the lone holdout
(`tools/lisp`) needs a conservative mark-sweep GC that assumes `ec`'s
stack-allocated globals — incompatible with ecomp's static-globals model.

`tools/oop-corpus.js` and `tools/lib-bakeoff.js` tabulate module linking
against the real `ec` oracle.

## Testing

```sh
npm test           # unit: lexer, parser, semantics, M68K encodings
npm run test:e2e   # end-to-end: the ecc CLI on fixture .e files
```

The e2e suite runs the CLI as a subprocess and asserts on artifacts:
hunk structure, embedded strings, **deterministic output**, `.m`
round-trips, multi-file builds, bootable ADF images, flag handling, and
error diagnostics. Both suites run in CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) on
node 16/20/22 — with zero dependencies there is no install step.

A third layer runs in CI as well: the **behavioral suite** compiles
fixture programs and executes the resulting Amiga binaries under vamos
(open-source m68k emulation), comparing stdout against golden outputs
that were verified byte-identical against the original 1997 compiler.

## How it works

```
src/lexer.js     tokens (E's case-classified identifiers, nested comments)
src/parser.js    AST  (line-continuation rules, no-precedence chains)
src/sem.js       symbol tables, const folding, object layouts, modules
src/codegen.js   M68K code generation + hand-assembled E runtime
src/asm68k.js    instruction encoder      src/asmtext.js  inline-asm assembler
src/emod.js      binary .m module reader  src/emodwrite.js  .m writer
src/hunk.js      AmigaOS executable       src/adf.js      bootable OFS floppy
```

Pure ES modules throughout; a unit test fails the build if anything under
`src/` touches a node API, which is what lets the identical code run
in the browser.

## License

GPL-3.0 (see `LICENSE`). **Exception:** `modules/` — the E v40 binary
modules — are copyright **Wouter van Oortmerssen**, included with his
explicitly granted permission, and are *not* relicensed by this project
(see `NOTICE`).

## Faithfulness notes (oracle-verified against real ec)

Runtime `*` and `/` are 16-bit (`fac(10)` really is -303360); only `x*2`
and `x*4` strength-reduce; `x++` advances by the pointed-to type's size;
`CONST` cannot reference other constants; `EXIT` is illegal in `LOOP`;
`EXCEPT DO` clears `exception` only on normal entry; `DisposeLink`
returns NIL; immediate lists are static and refilled on every evaluation.
See `tools/diff-test.js` for the full executable specification.

dosworld-zrdx-readme-md.text:
``` ______ ____ ______ __ |___ /| _ \| _ \ \/ / / / | |_) | | | \ / / /__| _ <| |_| / \ /_____|_| \_\____/_/\_\ ``` # 🔥 ZRDX — Zurenava DOS Extender 🔥 **A DOS4G/W-compatible 32-bit DOS extender — rebuilt with free tools, and still tiny.** [![License: CC0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-CC0%201.0-brightgreen?style=for-the-badge)](LICENSE) [![Platform](https://img.shields.io/badge/platform-MS--DOS-blue?style=for-the-badge&logo=windowsterminal&logoColor=white)](#-quick-start) [![Release](https://img.shields.io/badge/release-fix39-orange?style=for-the-badge)](docs/HISTORY.MD) [![DPMI](https://img.shields.io/badge/DPMI-0.9%20%E2%80%94%2049%2F49-red?style=for-the-badge)](docs/D09COV.MD) [![Assembler](https://img.shields.io/badge/core-NASM%20assembly-purple?style=for-the-badge)](#-building-from-source) **⚡ stub 14 KB ⚡ DPMI 0.9: 49 of 49 ⚡ VCPI / XMS / RAW ⚡ up to 4 GB ⚡ LE · PE · RDOFF2 ⚡** *Original author: Sergey Belyakov (1998-1999) Open source edition: DosWorld (2026)*
--- ## 🚀 What is it? ZRDX is a **DOS extender**: a tiny stub that is *bound* to the start of your 32-bit executable. The program starts, the stub switches the PC to protected mode, loads the main module and hands it a flat 32-bit world — exactly what DOS/4G(W) does, but small, free and hackable. No `DOS4GW.EXE` next to your program. 🎉 It is also a **standalone DPMI 0.9 host** (`zrxdpmi.exe`) for 16-bit and 32-bit clients. | | | |---|---| | 🎯 **Targets** | programs built for **DOS4G/W**, **PMODE/W**, **DOS32A**, **WDOSX** with Watcom C/C++, TMT Pascal, LadSoft C, … | | 📦 **Formats** | **LE** (DOS4G/W style), flat 32-bit **PE32** EXE (no imports, relocations supported), **RDOFF2** (`.rdf`, NASM + RLINK) | | 🧠 **Memory** | all physical memory (up to **4 GB**); in a test with 3000 MB RAM one `malloc` returned a 2995 MB block (DOS/4GW: 62 MB) | | 🔌 **DPMI** | **DPMI 0.9, all 49 specified INT 31h functions** — 42 full, 6 paging no-ops (memory is nonpageable), vendor lookup 0A00h without vendors. [Coverage report](docs/D09COV.MD) | | 🖥️ **Hosts** | runs under **DPMI**, **VCPI**, **XMS** and **RAW**; it picks what is available | | 🔁 **DOS calls** | translates everything PMODE/W translates (except identification) and almost all of DOS4G/W | | 📁 **Long names** | **LFN API** (int 21h, AX=71xxh) with buffer translation | | 📋 **Clipboard** | **Windows clipboard API** (int 2Fh, AX=17xxh), text and bitmaps translated both ways | | 📏 **Size** | every packed stub is **14 336 bytes** | | 🛠️ **Tools** | built with **NASM + Open Watcom + UPX** — no proprietary compilers | > 💡 The list of all translated DOS functions is in [`src/extender.asm`](src/extender.asm). --- ## ⚡ Quick start Everything you need is in [`bin/`](bin): | File | What it is | |---|---| | `zrxbind.com` | binds a ZRDX stub to your program (a 2 KB `.COM`) | | `stub-le.exe` | the stub for **LE** programs (DOS4G/W style) | | `stub-pe.exe` | the stub for **PE** programs | | `stub-rdf.exe` | the stub for **RDOFF2** (`.rdf`) programs | | `zrxsetup.exe` | changes the settings of a bound program | | `zrxdpmi.exe` | standalone **DPMI 0.9 host** (RAW / XMS / VCPI): `zrxdpmi PROGRAM.COM` | > ⚠️ `zrxbind.com` takes the stubs **only from its own directory** (found via the DOS > environment block, DOS 3.0+) — keep `zrxbind.com` and the `stub-*.exe` files together. > The stub is chosen by the format of the input file; you do not pick it. ```bat :: 1. build a 32-bit DOS4G/W-style program (Watcom example) wcl386 -l=dos4g -bt=dos hello.c :: 2. bind ZRDX to it zrxbind -c hello.exe hellz.exe :: 3. run it - no DOS4GW.EXE needed hellz.exe ``` ``` Zurenava DOS extender, version 0.52OSE. Copyright(C) 1998-1999, Sergey Belyakov Copyright(C) 2026, Viacheslav Komenda hello from 32-bit ``` Want a DPMI host for a separate DPMI client instead of binding? Run it through the host: ```bat zrxdpmi myclient.com :: the host owns discovery (1687h) for this command only ``` The first client fixes the bitness of the VM — do not mix 16-bit and 32-bit clients in one run. --- ## 🔗 Binding: `zrxbind` The stub is **bound to the start of the executable**. `zrxbind` looks at the input file and picks the stub: `LE` → `stub-le.exe`, `PE` → `stub-pe.exe`, `RDOFF2` → `stub-rdf.exe`. To put it on an already linked program use `-r` or `-c`: | Command | What it does | |---|---| | `zrxbind -r prog.exe` | **r**eplaces the old stub with ZRDX and makes a backup copy | | `zrxbind -r -n prog.exe` | the same, **n**o backup copy | | `zrxbind -c prog.exe out.exe` | **c**opies the program to a new file and binds ZRDX to it; the original stays untouched | | `zrxbind -w zrdx.exe` | **w**rites the **LE** stub itself to a file (a copy of `stub-le.exe`) | ```bat zrxbind -r -n doom.exe :: bind to doom.exe, no backup zrxbind -c doom.exe doomz.exe :: doomz.exe = doom.exe + ZRDX ``` ### 📚 The formats | Format | What the loader does | Limits | |---|---|---| | **LE** | loads objects, applies fixups, creates selectors (16/32-bit, flat) | as in DOS4G/W | | **PE** | allocates the image at any free address, loads sections, applies **base relocations** when the address differs from `ImageBase`, gives flat 4 GB code/data selectors, starts at the entry point | PE32/i386 EXE only; **no imports, DLLs, delay imports or TLS** (clear diagnostic); a `.reloc` directory is required unless the image lands on its `ImageBase`; stack = `SizeOfStackReserve` (64 KB … 4 MB) | | **RDOFF2** | loads `code`/`data`/`bss`, applies relocations, starts at the exported symbol `start` (or at the code start); a return stub is on the stack, so `RET` ends the program | single module: no `import`, `library`, `segrelo`, `farimport`; `EAX`/`EBX` = linear address of the code, `EDX` = linear address of the PSP | ```bat nasm -f rdf hello.asm -o hello.o :: 32-bit code, global start rlink rdf /o=hello.rdf hello.o :: see the RTools project zrxbind -c hello.rdf hello.exe :: stub-rdf.exe is used ``` Want ZRDX bound at **link time**? Extract the stub and give it to `wlink`: ```bat zrxbind -w zrdx.exe wlink ... option stub=zrdx.exe ``` --- ## 🔌 DPMI 0.9 coverage The built-in host was checked against the DPMI 0.9 specification (in [`docs/`](docs)): | Class | Calls | Notes | |---|---|---| | ✅ Full | **42** | descriptors, DOS memory, interrupts and exceptions, real-mode translation, callbacks, memory, physical mapping, virtual IF, **debug watchpoints 0B00h-0B03h** | | 🟡 No-op | **6** | 0600h-0603h, 0702h, 0703h: page lock / demand paging succeed, because memory is nonpageable | | 🔎 Lookup | **1** | 0A00h: optional vendor API lookup; no vendors, so every name returns CF=1 | **49 of 49** functions are in the dispatch table, for 16-bit and 32-bit clients. Current qualification: **55 native cases** and **17 bound API cases** on each of RAW, XMS and VCPI, 99 loader results and 11 tooling tests. Details, limits and evidence: [`docs/D09COV.MD`](docs/D09COV.MD), [`docs/D09WORK.MD`](docs/D09WORK.MD), [`docs/D09ABI.MD`](docs/D09ABI.MD). > Honest note: memory is **not swapped to disk**. A deferred plan exists > ([`docs/SWAPPLAN.MD`](docs/SWAPPLAN.MD)); the dormant `src/vmm.asm` is not qualified. --- ## 🎛️ Settings: `zrxsetup` ```bat zrxsetup [options] ``` `` is a program bound with `zrxbind`. Without switches `zrxsetup` prints the current configuration; with switches it prints what changes and writes the new values. | Switch | Meaning | Default | |---|---|---| | `/X` | max. XMS/RAW memory to allocate, in **KB** | `FFFFFFFF` | | `/L` | conventional memory to **leave free**, in paragraphs | `F000` | | `/T` | size of the DOS **transfer buffer**, in paragraphs (max `1000`) | `400` | | `/M<0/1>` | detection order: `0` = DPMI → VCPI, `1` = VCPI → DPMI | `0` | | `/B<0/1>` | startup copyright banner: `0` = off, `1` = on | `1` | | `/H`, `/?` | help | |
📖 What do these switches really do? (click) **`/X`** — RAW/XMS can't change the amount of memory on the fly, so the extender takes *all* free memory at start. If your program then runs another one (`exec`), the child gets no extended memory. If you plan to use `exec`, estimate what your program needs and set this value. In VCPI and DPMI modes there is no such problem: they allocate smartly. **`/L`** — when the DPMI server is initialised, all DOS memory minus this value joins the DPMI memory pool. Lowering it gives the client more memory. If you are going to `exec`, keep the default (`0F000h`). Close to `0` lets you run small programs even without extended memory. **`/T`** — DOS works only with low memory, but extended-mode parameters can be anywhere, so there is a buffer to carry data between the two worlds. A big read is split into chunks of this size. A bigger buffer means fewer calls and faster I/O, but less free low memory. **`/M`** — order of probing protected-mode interfaces. `0` = dpmi / vcpi / xms / raw (default), `1` = vcpi / dpmi / xms / raw. The first one that works wins. The standard recommends DPMI first, but some DPMI servers are buggy or provide VMM when it is not needed and only slow things down — that is why most extenders (DOS4G/W included) prefer VCPI when it is present. **`/B`** — no comment. *Banners must die!* 😄
### 💾 Where the settings live The settings are the **last 14 bytes of the bound program**: ``` offset size field ------ ---- ----------------------------------------------- -14 4 signature "ZRXC" -10 2 flags: bit 0 = banner off, bit 1 = VCPI before DPMI -8 2 transfer buffer size (paragraphs) -6 4 max. XMS/RAW memory (KB) -2 2 low memory to leave free (paragraphs) ``` `zrxbind` writes the default block; the stub reads it at start (it opens its own file anyway). Because it does not depend on the stub code, **the stub can be UPX-packed** and still be configured. Programs bound by an older `zrxbind` have no such block — bind them again. ### 🧩 Why so few switches? You may notice there are far fewer settings than in PMODE/W or DOS32A. The ZRDX kernel configures itself dynamically: - **Page tables** (and low memory) are allocated in VCPI mode on demand, always from the top of memory — the addressable space stays up to 4 GB. - **Physical-to-linear mappings** are allocated on demand, also up to 4 GB. - **LDT** starts with one page (511 selectors) and grows up to 8191. - **Stacks** are managed by an exclusive system and need no tuning. The only thing you may want to touch is the common DOS stack (you need just one); the default 512 bytes is plenty. - **Real-mode callbacks**: more than 20 will not work under DPMI, because most DPMI servers limit them to 20. --- ## 🛠️ Building from source Only **free tools**. No Borland C, no TASM, no TLINK, no MS link. | Tool | Version | Used for | |---|---|---| | [**NASM**](https://nasm.us/) | 3.01 on the host, 0.98.39 in DOS | the whole stub and the binder | | [**Open Watcom**](https://github.com/open-watcom/open-watcom-v2) | `wmake`, `wlink`, `wcl` | linking and the C tools | | [**UPX**](https://upx.github.io/) | 5.x (tested with 5.1.0) | packing the stubs, `zrxbind.com` and `zrxsetup` | Set the `WATCOM` environment variable, put the tools in `PATH` and run, in `src/`: ```bat wmake :: zrxbind.com, zrxsetup.exe and the stubs (stub-le/pe/rdf.exe) in binder\ wmake STUB=zrdx.exe PESTUB=zrdxpe.exe RDFSTUB=zrdxrdf.exe :: unpacked stubs wmake install :: copy zrxbind.com, zrxsetup.exe and the stubs to ..\bin wmake clean ``` `makefile` assembles with `NASMOPT = -O9` (accepted by NASM 0.98.39 and 3.x). The full reproducible build and check, which runs everything under DOSBox-X, is one command: ```sh python3 tests/CHECK.PY --work /tmp/ZRXWORK ``` The runner needs `ZRDX_DOSCONF` (a dosbox-x config), `ZRDX_DRIVE_C` (DOS tools) and `ZRDX_DRIVE_D` (Open Watcom); the scratch root `ZRDX_SCRATCH` defaults to `/tmp`. All variables, the native host, QEMU qualification, installation and reports: [`docs/BUILD.MD`](docs/BUILD.MD). Do not mix stubs from different builds. ### 🧪 Tests | Where | What | |---|---| | `tests/CHECK.PY` | the full runner: builds in scratch, runs all suites, writes `RESULT.JSN` | | `tests/rdf/` | about 50 self-checking programs for the RDF and LE loaders (each prints `ok` or `FAIL`) | | `tests/dpmi/` | native DPMI host fixtures, 55 cases, RAW / XMS / VCPI, QEMU for CPU-fault checks | | `tests/pe/`, `tests/mz/`, `tests/bind/` | generated PE, MZ-aligner and binder inputs, valid and damaged | | `tests/clip/` | clipboard mock | | `tests/mem/` | `malloc` size comparison with DOS/4GW and CauseWay | Covered: DPMI selectors, memory stress (random allocate/resize/free with patterns), out-of-memory, exception handlers, relocations, `start` lookup, PSP and registers at entry, 1 MB BSS, deep recursion, DOS file I/O larger than the transfer buffer, LFN and clipboard translation. ### 📏 Memory available to `malloc` `tests/mem` has a small Watcom C program (it prints the largest block one `malloc` can return) and batch files that build `memd.exe` (DOS/4GW), `memc.exe` (CauseWay) and `memz.exe` (ZRDX); see [`docs/MEMTEST.MD`](docs/MEMTEST.MD). In DOSBox-X with 3000 MB of RAM ZRDX gave one block of 2995 MB, DOS/4GW only 62 MB; CauseWay gave about 1 GB through its swap file (old measurement, recorded in [`docs/HISTORY.MD`](docs/HISTORY.MD)). ### 🔬 Experimental: VMM `src/vmm.asm` is a dormant virtual memory manager. It is **not** part of any release build and is not qualified. To try it, comment out `%assign Release 1` and uncomment `%assign VMM 1` in `segdefs.asm`. Known problems: pages are not freed under VCPI (use RAW/XMS), page unlocking is missing, and the swap file is reopened after each resize and not deleted on exit. Plan: [`docs/SWAPPLAN.MD`](docs/SWAPPLAN.MD). --- ## 🗂️ Repository ``` bin/ prebuilt: zrxbind.com, zrxsetup.exe, stub-le.exe, stub-pe.exe, stub-rdf.exe, zrxdpmi.exe (standalone DPMI host) src/ the sources (NASM) and the makefile zrdx.asm main file, includes everything (builds stub-le.exe) zrdxpe.asm PE stub root zrdxrdf.asm RDOFF2 stub root zrxdpmi.asm standalone DPMI host (with nathost.asm) gmacros.asm macros of virtual segments and labels segdefs.asm segment layout and sizes extender.asm DOS/BIOS call translation tables and handlers dpmifunc.asm DPMI functions (int 31h) realinit.asm, protinit.asm backend detection, entering PM prothand.asm, realhand.asm interrupts and mode switches mem.asm, smm.asm memory services (smm = active backend) leldr.asm / peldr.asm / rdfldr.asm LE, PE32, RDOFF2 loaders binder/ zrxbind.com source (bnd.asm, a .COM program) aligner/ stub aligner zrxsetup.c the settings utility tests/ CHECK.PY and the suites above docs/ BUILD.MD, D09COV.MD (DPMI coverage), backlog.txt, HISTORY.MD, plans history.txt changes by version LICENSE CC0 1.0 ``` Start with [`docs/README.MD`](docs/README.MD) — the project guide. --- ## 📜 History Version **0.52OSE**: the project moved to NASM + Open Watcom + UPX, the settings were moved to the end of the bound file, `zrxsetup` was rewritten, `zrxbind` became a `.COM` that reads the stubs from its directory, PE and RDOFF2 loaders were added. Current release **fix39**: DPMI 0.9 hardening and the native `zrxdpmi.exe` host, 14 336-byte packed stubs. See [`docs/HISTORY.MD`](docs/HISTORY.MD), the plans in [`docs/backlog.txt`](docs/backlog.txt) and [`history.txt`](history.txt). --- ## ⚠️ Notes and limitations - **Memory is not swapped to disk.** Swap-file paging is only a deferred plan ([`docs/SWAPPLAN.MD`](docs/SWAPPLAN.MD)). - **DPMI:** 0.9 only; DPMI 1.0 is not implemented and not planned. There are no vendor extensions (0A00h answers `CF=1`). - **PE:** one EXE, no imports, DLLs, delay imports or TLS. DLL loading is a deferred plan ([`docs/PEPLAN.MD`](docs/PEPLAN.MD)). - **How it was verified:** the full campaign (55 native, 17 bound, 99 loader results) was recorded on the reference machine on 2026-10-18 under DOSBox-X and QEMU. CPU-fault checks and the VCPI debug-watch checks need QEMU with a FreeDOS image, which is not shipped. DOSBox-X alone cannot run them. On 2026-10-20 the PE loader (including relocations, 24 cases) and a fresh rebuild of all six binaries were re-checked; the QEMU campaign was not repeated. - **Test setup is local:** the runners take DOSBox-X, the DOS tool tree, Open Watcom and the disk image from environment variables (see above); none of them is shipped. - **Recorded source fingerprint:** `docs/TOOLS.JSN` holds the source hash from 2026-10-18; sources changed afterwards but a rebuild gives byte-identical binaries. - **Specifications in `docs/`** (`DPMI09.HTM`, `DPMI10.TXT`, `VCPI.TXT`) are third-party documents kept for reference. Their copyright stays with the original owners; the CC0 license applies to the ZRDX sources only. - **`src/vmm.asm` is experimental** and not part of any release build. --- ## ⚖️ License [CC0 1.0](LICENSE). ZRDX was distributed by its author as **freeware**: it can be freely copied and used for any purpose, commercial or not, and there are no restrictions on software built by modifying or extending the ZRDX sources or binaries. ZRDX is distributed **"AS IS"** — the author does not guarantee fitness for any particular purpose and is not responsible for any consequences of using or not using this product. ## 🙏 Credits - **Sergey Belyakov** — author of ZRDX (1998-1999), homepage `http://www.zrdx.da.ru` - **DosWorld** — open source edition (2026)
**Made with 🔥 for the DOS people.** · Banners must die! · Long live protected mode!

sidecartridge-gemdrive-game-patches-read.text:
# Atari ST hard-disk adaptations, from GEMDOS and GEMDRIVE

The 8bitchip.info website lists 1,831 Atari ST games adapted to start from a hard disk. This
project starts every one of them from a **GEMDOS drive**, a folder that the ST sees as drive C:,
served file by file with no disk sectors: the Hatari emulator's GEMDOS drive, and the
[SidecarTridge Multi-device](https://sidecartridge.com/products/sidecartridge-multidevice-atari-st/)'s
**GEMDRIVE** on real machines. Most games run as they are. The others need a fix, and this
repository builds the fixes.

**To use it, go to <https://gemdrive.sidecartridge.com/>, "Patch a game".** Give it a game's ZIP
exactly as downloaded from the 8bitchip.info website: it says whether the game runs as it is, and
when a fix makes it run, it patches the ZIP in your browser and gives it back. This README is for
developers.

## What it found

- 1,608 games run from GEMDOS and GEMDRIVE as they are.
- 212 need a fix. 209 of them run with this project's fixes, in Hatari and on real machines with
  the Multi-device.
- 1 is not feasible, and 10 are still unsure.

Most of the games to fix use the Gamex launcher with GOS4 or GOS5: their own GEMDOS, a copy of TOS
1.04's that runs from RAM and reads the hard disk sector by sector through the `PPDRIVER` driver. A
GEMDOS drive has no driver and no sectors. The fix rebuilds the game's start program so that GOS
asks the drive for its files by name instead. Three smaller fixes cover eight other games.

## No original files

The games, their adaptations and their documentation belong to the 8bitchip.info website, a third
party. This repository and its website carry none of their files: no game, no launcher, no ZIP. The
fixes are our own code, and the patcher rebuilds the fixed file from the user's own download,
checked against this project's build by SHA-256. The tables keep each download's name, size and
hash only.

## The pieces

- **The survey** (`tools/survey/`): every game of the list, its files, its strategy (the way its
  adaptation reaches its files), its run in Hatari and its verdict (`src/survey/migration.csv`).
- **The fixes**:
  - S1, the GOS5 and GOS4 games: `tools/build_gos5.py`, `tools/build_gos4.py`, with our blocks
    `src/gemdrive/gos5_patch.s` and `gos4_patch.s`.
  - S2, a BPB for the drive: `GDBPB.PRG`, from `src/gemdrive/gdbpb.s`.
  - S3, the fastload bit: `tools/set_fastload.py`.
  - S4, a missing start program: `tools/rody2_runme.py`.
- **The patcher** (`tools/site/patcher.js`): the fixes in JavaScript, byte for byte the Python
  tools' results, run in the browser on the user's ZIP; its table is `src/survey/patches.tsv`
  (`tools/survey/patch_table.py`).
- **The website** (`tools/site/`): the findings, the modes, the solutions, the patcher and the
  catalogue of every game.
- **The reverse engineering** (`src/`): the maps of the Lemmings launcher's stages, from which
  `tools/make_sources.sh` makes sources that reassemble to the original bytes, using your own copy
  of the game in `LEMMINGS/`; and the notes (`src/notes/`).

## Building and testing

You need Python 3, Docker with the pinned toolchain image, and Hatari 2.6.1 with the TOS images.
Copy `tools/dev/dev.cfg.example` to `tools/dev/dev.cfg` and set its paths, then:

```
tools/dev/all_harness.sh                        # every check: disks, round trip, Hatari runs, the site
python3 tools/build_gos5.py START.TOS OUT.TOS   # a GOS5 game's start program, built for a GEMDOS drive
python3 tools/build_gos4.py START.TOS OUT.TOS   # the same for a GOS4 game
python3 tools/survey/sdcard.py                  # every game laid out for a microSD card, fixes applied
python3 tools/survey/patch_table.py             # the patcher's table of every archive
python3 tools/site/build_site.py --check        # the website, into tools/dev/builds/site/
make tag                                        # the release: the website published, version.txt tagged
```

Every fix is tested twice: in Hatari, on an emulated ST with TOS 1.04 and STE with TOS 1.62 and
2.06, from its GEMDOS drive and from a `PPDRIVER` hard-disk image as the reference; then on real
machines with the Multi-device's GEMDRIVE, from a test card. Hatari's GEMDOS drive and GEMDRIVE
behave the same on every machine; only the exceptions are reported. `tools/dev/README.md` has the
whole toolset, and `CLAUDE.md` the working rules.

## The website

The website is <https://gemdrive.sidecartridge.com/> (`CNAME`). `python3 tools/site/build_site.py`
writes it into `tools/dev/builds/site/`; it works from that folder and needs nothing from another
site. `--check` verifies every link and anchor, every game's row, and that no page loads another
site's files. CI runs it on every pull request and push to `main`. `tools/site/deploy_site.sh`
publishes it, with the screenshots of this project's Hatari runs, on the `gh-pages` branch.

## Licence

GNU General Public License v3.0; see [LICENSE](LICENSE). The games and their adaptations are not
covered by it, and are not part of this repository.

robbiew-yankeetrader-readme-md.text:
# Yankee Trader: Resurrection

Version **0.1.0**, with the original game by Alan Davenport, based on Yankee Trader Version 3.6. A reconstruction for local play and BBS doors, built with Go/GoDoors. The first playable milestone supports persistent players, sector navigation, cloak-aware adjacent-sector sensors, directed path finding and confirmed autopilot, cargo trading, Earth equipment purchases, automatic saves, and planet creation, production, transfers and banking, plus port buyouts, personal treasury collection, teams/shared planets, and daily port/planet production and turn maintenance. The original DOS distribution and research evidence are untouched. The app name, semantic version, original creator and version, and repository link come from [`internal/version`](internal/version/version.go); run `./bin/yt -version` to display the release identity.

## A little history

Yankee Trader is Alan Davenport's text-based BBS space strategy game, combining
exploration, trading and warfare. Its roots are in the Trade Wars 2 code base:
following Chris Sherrick's first Trade Wars in 1984, Davenport released Trade
Wars 1000 in 1987. The game took the Yankee Trader name in 1989, and its final
DOS release, version 3.6, arrived in 1994.

[Zharous's Yankee Trader strategy guide](https://yt.starflt.com/22-2/) records
that history and reports that Davenport's original QuickBASIC source was lost.
This project reconstructs the game in Go using the preserved DOS distribution
and captured behavior as references.

## DOS-style startup

The default interface adapts the preserved DOS title and opening art with
Resurrection branding, and reproduces the new-player
alias confirmation, instructions choice, ship-information pause, sector display
and first command menus. Use an 80×25 ANSI terminal for the recovered colors and
layout. Local terminals receive UTF-8 box characters; ANSI BBS callers receive
raw CP437. Door32's emulation field selects the remote display; `-ascii` forces
plain text. No terminal-size probes are required.

Press a key at the title, then a separate key after the opening artwork. Each
page stays visible until its own keypress. New players enter an in-game alias (Enter uses the
Door32 real name, or the local name), confirm with `Y`, and choose whether to read
the original instructions. Press a key after ship information. At the main
prompt, Enter redisplays the sector, `?` shows the original two-column help,
`C` enters the ship's computer, and `Q` asks for confirmation. Commands finish
with Enter and can be stacked with semicolons. A trailing `/` saves a command
line for Ctrl-R replay; `/R2` through `/R20` repeat a command.

In this interface `L` follows DOS and lands on a planet; `LOOK` displays the
sector. The compact interface keeps its existing `L` look binding. Use
`-compact` to skip the startup screens and retain the prior command workflow.
The computer currently connects options 3 (autopilot), 7 (avoid slots), and 10
(path finder) to the implemented game rules.

The original menus and manual include features still under reconstruction.
Selecting an unavailable action says so; radio, scanner and cloak values are
not fabricated. Ship balances and inventory come from the current Go world,
including its existing deliberate differences from DOS starting equipment.
The startup screens identify this project as Yankee Trader: Resurrection
0.1.0, say “Original game by Alan Davenport” and “Based on Yankee Trader
Version 3.6,” and link to the
[GitHub repository](https://github.com/robbiew/yankeetrader). No registration
code is required. Original DOS artwork remains preserved in the archive.

See [startup evidence and limits](research/yt-startup/RECOVERY.md) and the
[title](evidence/startup/title.png), [ship information](evidence/startup/info.png),
and [main menu](evidence/startup/help.png) captures.

## Play locally

From the repository directory, build the game, create a world, and start a local
session (see [Build and validate](#build-and-validate) for prerequisites):

```sh
go build -o bin/yt ./cmd/yt
./bin/yt -data data -init
./bin/yt -data data -local Player
```

On Windows, build with `-o bin/yt.exe` and use `.\bin\yt.exe` in place of
`./bin/yt`. Replace `Player` with your local player name. For later sessions,
run only the local-play command with the same name and data directory.

For a separate new world, run `./bin/yt -data another-world -init`. Initialization refuses to overwrite an existing world; skip that step if you already have one. `-local` is for trusted local play; do not give remote callers control over that flag or the data directory. The data files live in `data`, separately from the DOS game. Every successful action saves before its result is displayed. Quitting or disconnecting never restores spent resources or turns.

Try this route to buy a fighter, buy five ore at sector 2, and sell it at sector 3:

```text
P; EQUIP fighters 1; M 2; P; BUY ore 5; M 3; P; SELL ore 5; I; Q
```

The expected starting-player result is 1,005 credits, 26 fighters, no cargo, sector 3, and 495 turns. Terminal commands are case-insensitive and can be stacked with semicolons.

| Command | Action |
|---|---|
| `?` | Help |
| `I` | Ship information |
| `LOOK` | Current sector, warps, and port (`L` in compact mode) |
| `M <sector>` | Move through a listed adjacent warp; one turn |
| `S` / `SCAN` | Scan adjacent sectors: ports, planets, ships and outgoing warps; free |
| `PATH <from> <to>` | Display a shortest directed warp route and turn cost; free |
| `AUTO <sector>` | Plot from your current sector, confirm with Y/N, then move one turn per hop |
| `AVOID` | Show your saved routing preferences; free |
| `AVOID <slot> <sector>` | Set slot 1–30; sector 0 clears that slot; free |
| `P` | Dock and display current prices; one turn |
| `T` / `TEAM` | Team menu: create/join, roster/resources, leave and captain controls |
| `B` / `ACQUIRE` | Buy the current port after explicit `Y` confirmation |
| `TREASURY` / computer `C`, `12` | Report personally owned port balances |
| `$` / `COLLECT` | Collect all personal port balances from any sector |
| `BUY ore 5` / `SELL ore 5` | Trade cargo in the direction the port supports |
| `EQUIP fighters 1` | Buy equipment while docked at Earth |
| `LEAVE` | Leave port |
| `Q` or Escape | Exit |

Sensors work even when no turns remain. `AUTO` asks before moving; an empty answer cancels. You can stack the response, for example `PATH 1 3; AUTO 3; Y; I`. Ctrl-X stops autopilot between hops. Every completed hop saves immediately and remains spent after interruption or disconnect. Courses stop if another session changes your position or leaves too few turns. See [navigation recovery and DOS comparisons](research/yt-navigation/RECOVERY.md).

`PATH` and `AUTO` honor your 30 private avoid slots, including the start and destination. For example, `AVOID 1 2` routes around sector 2; `AVOID 1 0` clears that preference. Manual `M` movement and sensors still work normally. Avoid edits cost no turns and persist across logins—an intentional improvement over the DOS session-only list. If a list edit makes a plotted course unsafe, autopilot stops before the next hop and keeps completed moves saved. Existing saves begin with an empty list.

Sensors show actual public sector/ship data. Defense deployment, danger scanners and manual emergency warps remain outside this slice. Minefields and safe automatic escape are implemented in the later milestones below. Cloak detection and direct fighter attacks are implemented in the later milestones below. Default worlds start without minefields; non-Earth combat wrecks can create them.

The default planet interface now follows the original DOS landing/report, help and transfer menus, with cyan text, original columns, gray answers and captured warning/receipt colors. Press `L` to land (or create a planet when none exists), `?` for planet help, `D` to redisplay, `N` to rename, `1`–`6`/`9` to take an item, Enter/`A` to take all, `T` to deposit items, `B` for the bank, `$` to invest, `F` to set the planetary garrison, and `L` to leave. Bank and garrison prompts ask for a **final target**, not a transfer amount. Empty bank/investment/garrison inputs cancel; empty take quantities choose the displayed maximum. Planet creation requires purchase and name confirmation. Thrusters and forced landing are not implemented yet. See [37 captured planet stages and comparison boundaries](research/yt-planet-screens/RECOVERY.md).

Planet renaming uses the original name/confirmation prompts and colors. Blank names cancel; `N` at confirmation retries; Enter accepts. Names receive DOS word casing/space cleanup and are clipped to 41 characters. Renaming costs no credits or turns and uses the current landing permission, including shared/unguarded access. Reserved names and the final special planet slot remain protected. See [rename rules, 45 DOS captures and comparison boundaries](research/yt-planet-rename/RECOVERY.md).

Port colors, commodity columns, dotted labels, Earth menu spacing, and purchase prompts are checked against 35 original DOS screen captures from ten isolated sessions. The comparisons cover the port body through the current prompt, including Earth redraws, purchases, sales, ownership, full holds, and declined trades. Live timestamps and unsupported-item affordability remain dynamic; startup history, caller/status details, timing, and invalid-input behavior are outside this visual comparison. See [port screen evidence](research/yt-port-screens/RECOVERY.md).

In the default DOS-style interface, `P` opens Earth's numbered shop or the current port's cargo report. Earth keeps the original item numbers: `2` holds, `3` fighters, `7` ground forces, `8` shields, `I` ship information, and `0` leave. Other historical equipment options retain their original labels and prices, with `N/A` affordability; selecting one reports that it is unavailable. An empty equipment quantity cancels that purchase. The shop refreshes your credits after each saved purchase.

Ordinary ports offer commodities in ore/organics/equipment order. Enter a quantity (`0` skips), then agree with `Y` or Enter; `N` declines. Enter at the quantity prompt selects the displayed maximum, limited by current stock/demand, cargo space, cargo aboard, and credits. Invalid quantities skip that commodity without a transaction. Docking costs one turn, including a visit with no purchases. A replaced or expired docking session cannot complete an old prompt. `-compact` keeps the explicit `BUY`, `SELL`, and `EQUIP` workflow.

Other cargo names are `organics` and `equipment`. Earth sells `holds` (500 credits), `fighters` (100), `shields` (50), and `forces` (750). Quantities must be whole, positive numbers. Cargo capacity is shared across all three cargo types. Earth equipment costs remain an economic sink.

## Run as a BBS door

Use the directory containing that node's Door32 drop file and the same absolute data directory on every node:

```sh
/path/to/yankeetrader/bin/yt \
  -data /path/to/yankeetrader/data \
  -drop /path/to/node1 \
  -system mybbs
```

`-system` is a stable namespace for the BBS. Identity uses this value plus the positive user-record number on Door32 line five; alias is display information. Changing an alias does not create a fresh ship. Keep the system value stable. Local identities are separate from Door32 identities.

GoDoors handles standard I/O on macOS/Linux and inherited Door32 sockets on supported Windows hosts. The door honors the drop file's remaining session time (1–1,440 minutes). The DOS-style interface supports ANSI/CP437 and plain text; `-compact` retains the original printable-ASCII command interface. Neither requires terminal probing.

Native macOS PTY and Door32 **local transport** were exercised. Linux/Windows builds compile, but this is not evidence of live acceptance under either BBS transport. Test an inherited Windows socket on the target BBS before deployment.

## Daily maintenance

```sh
./bin/yt -data data -maint
```

Port purchases cost `floor(sum of production / 10) + 1` credits and no turns. Buying an owned port pays its former owner the price plus its treasury, then clears that account. Earth cannot be bought. Confirmation defaults to cancellation and expires after five minutes; changed ownership, location, price or funds rejects the sale. Ownership changes invalidate docking agreements in the sector. Treasury collection is free, remote and personal; insufficient credit capacity rejects the entire collection. See [ownership evidence and deliberate fixes](research/yt-trade/OWNERSHIP.md).

Maintenance runs automatically at login as well. Days use **UTC**. On a new date it updates port supply, taxes ordinary port treasuries by `floor(treasury/10)`, restores players to 500 turns, and invalidates outstanding docking sessions. Repeating the command on the same day, or moving the clock backward, does not repeat daily phases. A missed interval gets at most ten days of port production; missing days do not accumulate extra player turns. Taxes run once when advancing the maintenance marker, not once for every missed day.

Planet maintenance also produces stocks and weapons, grows rates and ground defenses, and pays bank interest. NPC actions, deletion, lottery and other daily phases remain deferred. Cloak decay follows turn spending, rather than daily maintenance.

## Fidelity and deliberate changes

Implemented rules have links to the recovered evidence:

- Starting 1,005 credits, 25 fighters, 10 holds and 500 daily turns: [initializer evidence](research/dos-validation/RESULTS.md).
- Supply-sensitive cargo prices, quantity limits, demand depletion and owner commissions: [trading recovery](research/yt-trade/RECOVERY.md). Five saved DOS examples are exported in `internal/game/testdata/dos-trading.json` and checked by Go tests. These compare ore cash/cargo/treasury outcomes; they do not claim exact QuickBASIC RNG or floating-point equivalence.
- Port taxes and the repeated-maintenance defect: [maintenance recovery](research/yt-maint/RECOVERY.md).

Universe generation is a new seeded, reachable graph, not the recovered DOS generator. Default size is 3,000 sectors and 1,000 ports; `-sectors` allows 8–3,000 for small test games. Ports alternate cargo types and use fixed reference prices **20/30/40** until the DOS reference-price RNG is fully established. Shields start at zero in this prototype; shield initialization parity remains outside this milestone.

Known defects intentionally fixed here:

- Spendable money is `int64`, preserving one-credit debits at large balances across saves. It never uses MBF single precision.
- Earth cannot have an owner, and equipment spending cannot fund an owner treasury.
- Clock rollback preserves the last production watermark; it never awards ten days of goods.
- Daily phases have an actual persisted guard against same-day repeats.
- Each action loads authoritative state under the world lock. Failed actions commit nothing.
- Dock tokens expire after five minutes and are invalidated by movement, another docking, reconnect, or maintenance. Old sessions cannot apply a previous quote after another session changes the player's position.

Technical limits are 50 players, 1,000 cargo holds, 1 billion units per noncargo equipment category, and 9 quadrillion credits per account. These bounds are explicit prototype constraints, not claims about DOS overflow behavior.

Sector-defense deployment/combat and reinforcement, NPCs, full universe generation parity, DOS save import/export, Genesis, and richer terminal menus remain future milestones. Their recovered rules are in `research`.

## Storage and recovery

**Save rollback compatibility:** This build uses world version 8 for missile deaths and a stored score cache, alongside attributed minefields and persisted cloak energy, in addition to loot/estate settlement and optional sector defenses. Existing version-1/version-2 saves with no team memberships and normal version-3/version-4/version-5/version-6/version-7 saves upgrade in memory and persist on the next successful update; read-only loading does not rewrite them. Experimental legacy membership IDs without team metadata are rejected. Older binaries cannot read version 8. Back up the data directory with the door stopped, upgrade every node together, and restore the matching backup if reverting binaries. Restoring a backup discards later progress. Existing aliases, identities, assets, balances, login dates and avoid lists are preserved.

`world.json` is the versioned authoritative save. `world.lock` is a persistent lock-file name backed by an OS lock: process death releases the lock without deleting it. All processes must use the same data directory on a local filesystem. Network filesystems are not supported or tested.

Updates serialize through the lock, validate the complete world, write and sync a temporary file, then replace the save atomically on macOS/Linux. The containing directory is also synced there. Windows uses its file lock and replacement APIs but has not received native crash/durability acceptance. Orphan `.world-*` files are never treated as committed saves. Existing/corrupt saves are never silently reinitialized. Back up the data directory while the door is stopped, or take a filesystem snapshot.

If a save error occurs, stop and inspect the filesystem before retrying a purchase: an error syncing the directory after replacement can mean the new state is visible even though durability was not confirmed.

## Build and validate

Requires Go 1.23+ and a local GoDoors checkout at commit [`9364a49ddd7c396ccbfcdd3c240c104ea9178551`](https://github.com/robbiew/godoors/commit/9364a49ddd7c396ccbfcdd3c240c104ea9178551) or a descendant. That revision includes the timed-input API and preserves partial escape sequences across the 1 ms autopilot polls. `go.mod` currently replaces `github.com/robbiew/godoors` with `../godoors`, matching this workspace. For another checkout, point that replacement at the matching GoDoors source before building. No changes were made to the GoDoors repository.

```sh
go build -o bin/yt ./cmd/yt
go test -race ./...
go vet ./...
python3 scripts/smoke.py
python3 scripts/smoke_startup.py
python3 scripts/smoke_prompt_clock.py
python3 scripts/verify_port_screens.py
python3 scripts/smoke_port_parity.py
python3 scripts/verify_planet_screens.py
python3 scripts/smoke_planet_parity.py
python3 scripts/smoke_planet_parity.py --ascii
python3 scripts/verify_planet_rename.py
python3 scripts/smoke_planet_rename.py
python3 scripts/smoke_planet_rename.py --ascii
python3 scripts/verify_startup_evidence.py
python3 scripts/smoke_navigation.py
python3 scripts/verify_navigation_evidence.py
python3 scripts/verify_avoid_evidence.py
```

The smoke script also exercises planet creation, banking, investment, cargo transfers and reconnect. The smoke script uses a disposable world and real PTYs. It exercises GoDoors input/output, trading, equipment, movement, reconnect, repeated maintenance and Door32 local sessions with an alias change. Transcript: [local smoke evidence](evidence/local-smoke.txt).

The tests also cover rejected-action rollback, malformed saves, competing goroutines/processes, a killed lock holder, stale docking tokens, exact-money persistence, and DOS trading examples. Successful cross-compilation is recorded separately from native runtime/BBS validation in [validation evidence](evidence/VALIDATION.md).

## Planet management

The explicit commands below apply to `-compact`. The default interface uses the DOS planet menus described above.

`CREATE <name>` spends 25,000 credits and creates a planet in the current sector (one per sector, slots 2–100). It starts with production rates 1/1/1, stocks 10/10/10, 30 fighters, ground defense 1 and an empty bank. Creation does not land the ship or spend a turn.

| Command | Action |
|---|---|
| `LAND` / `PLANET` | Land, or display the landed planet |
| `BANK <target>` | Set the bank balance; move the difference to/from ship credits |
| `INVEST <credits>` | Spend credits to add credits/250 to each production rate |
| `TRANSFER cargo` | Unload all ship cargo; apply the recovered stock-based rate improvement |
| `TRANSFER fighters [quantity]` | Unload fighters; omitted quantity means all |
| `TRANSFER missiles [quantity]` | Unload missiles; mines and plasma work the same way |
| `TAKE <item> <quantity>` | Load whole units of cargo or weapons |
| `A` / `TAKEALL` | Load equipment, organics, ore in that order, then weapons |
| `GARRISON <target>` | Set planetary ground forces using the ship's ground forces; zero releases ownership |
| `LEAVE` | Leave the planet or port |

Owners, members of the same nonzero team, and visitors to unguarded planets can land. Permission and current position are rechecked on every action. Team assignment and planetary combat are not implemented yet.

Production uses elapsed time capped at ten days. Visiting grows rates before production; daily maintenance produces before growing rates, matching the two recovered DOS paths. Banking reevaluates surplus production after changing the balance. Fractional stock is retained; only whole units move aboard. See [planet recovery](research/yt-combat/RECOVERY.md) and the packaged reports in `research/yt-combat` for the original evidence (report filenames are preserved).

Money remains exact integer credits, including interest. This deliberately fixes the DOS large-balance banking exploit: even a one-credit deposit debits the ship. Empty transfers cannot increase production; failed or competing actions cannot duplicate goods. Clock rollback preserves the production watermark. Movement, reconnect and maintenance invalidate landing authorization.

Version-1 through version-7 worlds upgrade to version 8 in memory and are saved atomically on the next successful update, preserving existing players and assets. The local `data` and `bin` directories are ignored by Git. The original DOS distribution and full recovery workspace are preserved under `archive/`; portable supporting reports and compressed DOS snapshots are included under `research`.

## Complete recovery archive

The [complete archive](archive/README.md) includes the original DOS distribution, full experiments, Ghidra projects, player spreadsheet and [art/menu gallery](archive/analysis/art-menus/index.html). Run `python3 scripts/verify_archive.py` to verify all imported checksums. This repository is the working home for future recovery; the old Downloads folder is no longer required.

On exit, the original DOS tune plays only when GoDoors positively identifies
SyncTERM or another CTerm-compatible terminal using its device-attributes query.
Unknown terminals and `-ascii` sessions receive no music bytes. Music uses the
CTerm `CSI |` introducer and SO/SI terminators, avoiding the legacy `CSI M`
sequence that ordinary ANSI terminals interpret as delete-line.

## Teams

Press `T` (or `TEAM`) for the team menu. Create a team with a name of 3–41 printable characters and a four-character invitation password, or select a listed team to join. Passwords are case-insensitive, entered separately at a masked prompt, and stored as bcrypt hashes. Do not stack passwords with commands. Teams hold up to four members; joining and team management spend no credits or turns.

Members can view the roster and teammate planet locations, share defended teammate planets, and confirm departure. New deaths also remove membership. Only the current captain can rename the team, change its invitation or remove another member. Removal permits rejoining until the password changes. If the captain leaves, the next member to visit the menu or log in succeeds them. Empty teams disappear.

Leaving or removal immediately revokes shared landing sessions that no longer have access. Planets and ports retain their individual owners; port treasuries remain personal. Sector defenses can be deployed/recovered with `F`/`DEFEND`, and teammates may reinforce them with `REINFORCE` or team option 6. See [team implementation and evidence](research/yt-teams/IMPLEMENTATION.md).

## Combat preparation

Confirmed direct fighter attacks are now available; minefield aftermath is implemented, with sector-defense combat available as described below. The engine now records death and replacement atomically and binds each logged-in session to its ship generation. Old commands and pending prompts cannot act after death or use a replacement ship. Fresh-login replacement preserves remaining turns, while ordinary daily maintenance remains the only turn refill. Self-death has a next-UTC-day cooldown; enemy retaliation keeps its actual killer attribution. These internal transitions have no production kill/debug command. See [lifecycle scope, policies and validation](research/yt-ships/LIFECYCLE.md). Internal fighter/shield calculations, sampled inventory salvage and complete modeled estate transfers are implemented; player-facing fighter attacks connect these operations, including attributed minefield aftermath outside Earth. [Duel and settlement scope](research/yt-ships/DUELS.md).

## Loot and death-related ownership

Internal settlement samples holds, money and weapons separately, then chooses cargo from the salvaged holds. Awards consume the victim's inventory exactly once. Recipient limits reject the complete transaction, and cash stays integer-based throughout sampling and transfer.

A new enemy death transfers ordinary ports with their treasuries intact. Self/environmental death releases those ports and clears their treasuries. Planets remain owned by the victim. Death removes team membership and revokes shared guarded-planet access; owned sector fighters become Mercenaries. Captured/released ports invalidate old docking agreements. Replacement preserves remaining turns and retained planets.

Sector defenses have deployment/recovery, reinforcement, confirmed combat and missile interception, with real sensor reports and hostile-warp blocking. Default worlds have no deployed defenses. Direct fighter attacks are enabled for supported encounters. Non-Earth wreck mines now form attributed minefields and resolve against the attacker. Earth safely disposes of its unsalvaged mines. [Settlement rules, upgrades and validation](research/yt-ships/SETTLEMENT.md).

Cloak energy persists per ship, decays by one percentage point when a spent turn
leaves a multiple of 25 turns, and starts full on new/replacement ships. Legacy
saves retain zero cloak. Sensor detection is private to each session and never
drains the observed ship. See [cloak scope and validation](research/yt-ships/CLOAK.md).

### Confirmed fighter attacks

Use `ATTACK` to list visible local enemies and choose a ship number and committed
fighters, or `ATTACK <ship number> <fighters>`. Classic main-menu `A` enters this
dialog; the planet-menu `A` take-all binding is retained. A separate exact `Y`
confirms one attack. Blank, N, Escape or disconnect cancels; stacked answers,
queued keys and command-repeat syntax cannot supply approval. Fighters, defenses,
loot and ownership save together, and direct fighter attacks spend no turns.

Earth safely disposes of unsalvaged victim mines after loot is consumed once.
Mine-bearing targets outside Earth are enabled, with wreck drops and chained
deaths resolved atomically. Other supported direct duels are available; one-hop missile attacks and counterfire are implemented below; sector-defense combat is available below. See [scope and validation](research/yt-ships/PLAYER_ATTACKS.md).

### Minefields and chained deaths

Non-Earth wrecks drop only unsalvaged carried mines, once, with their source
account retained. Mines threaten all occupants, including their source and team.
Manual entry requires a fresh warning confirmation; autopilot stops before a
mined hop. Sensors report the actual stock. Current-sector hazards resolve before
commands or on reconnect, and save-lock guards prevent spending or moving away
through a newly arrived field. Small surviving ships may emergency-warp to a
safe destination even with no remaining turns.

Mine deaths retain their actual source even if that source already died. They
release ports rather than award remote loot, and do not become voluntary suicides.
Earth remains free of mines. This build now uses save version 8; follow the stopped-world
backup and all-node upgrade guidance. Mine placement/withdrawal commands and wider missile encounters remain separate;
sector-fighter combat is available below. See [rules and validation](research/yt-ships/MINES.md).

### Missile attacks and retaliation

Use `MISSILE <adjacent sector> <quantity>` or classic `!`; omitted arguments are
prompted. Launches need a fresh separate Y and cost one turn plus all selected
missiles. This stage supports a one-hop corridor linked in both directions, with
one visible enemy ship, a minefield or a hostile fighter group. Hidden ships and teammates are skipped.
Hostile planets support ground-only bombardment as described below. Longer routes,
multiple visible enemies and mixed visible ship/planet encounters remain blocked.

Hostile sector fighters intercept missiles first (up to 4,999 fighters per missile); friendly groups are bypassed. Remaining missiles clear one mine each before reaching the ship. A surviving enemy with
missiles returns one volley against the original attacker, including through
its cloak; return fire does not consume that defender's daily turns or recurse.
Both volleys, loot, deaths, port transfers and mine drops save together.
Remaining outgoing missiles clear wreck mines before dissipating. Earth disposal
still applies. A ship whose shields reach zero is destroyed even if escorts
remain, as in the recovered missile path. Prototype new ships still start with
zero shields: purchase shields at Earth before combat.

Return-volley sizing uses the saved `StoredScore` cache. New/migrated accounts
start at zero and use the recovered random 1..stock fallback; score calculation
and scoreboard maintenance are not implemented yet. No wealth-derived score is
invented. Positive cached scores use the recovered score formula. See
[missile scope, rules and validation](research/yt-missiles/IMPLEMENTATION.md).

### Sector fighters

`F <total>` / `DEFEND <total>` sets the final size of your current-sector defense;
`F 0` recovers it. Deployment is prohibited in Union sectors 1–7. Existing legacy
groups there may be reduced or recovered. `REINFORCE <quantity>` and team option 6
add fighters to an existing personal or teammate group without changing ownership.
Only its owner may recover a group; all transfers enforce ship and defense capacity.

Hostile defenses stop ordinary movement. Use `BREACH <current-or-adjacent sector>
<fighters>` to commit a force. Choose whether to accept human surrender, then give
a fresh separate Y to fight. Surviving defenders may surrender when outnumbered
strictly more than ten to one; NPCs and Mercenaries refuse. Uncommitted fighters
stay aboard. Exhausting the committed force forces emergency escape; `FLEE` also
escapes a current hostile group, with a fresh confirmation and possible loss of
all remaining turns. Adjacent entry spends one movement turn. Victory resolves
any destination mines in the same saved transaction. Defeating a group does not
kill its owner or capture a port. [Rules, policies and validation](research/yt-combat/SECTOR_FIGHTERS.md).

### Planetary ground bombardment

`MISSILE <adjacent sector> <quantity>` can strike a hostile planet after sector
fighters and mines intercept the volley. A fresh warning names the planet and
its garrison. Own/team planets and mixed visible ship/planet encounters are blocked.
The selected quantity must be at most the planet's saved ground forces divided
by 25 (rounded down), ensuring every missile stays in the recovered ground phase.
Ground below 25 and volleys that could reach production remain unsupported.
Planet growth runs before impact; the remaining fractional ground balance is
rounded down once at the end. The launch, interception, growth and ground damage save together. Planet
ownership stays unchanged. [Rules, evidence and remaining work](research/yt-missiles/GROUND_BOMBARDMENT.md).

# Scorched Earth - HTML5 / TypeScript Port A browser reimplementation of **Scorched Earth v1.5** (1995, DOS) by **Wendell Hicken** - "The Mother of All Games" - running natively on TypeScript + Canvas2D + Web Audio. No plugins, no WASM, no Python or DOS runtime: open it and play. ### Play it now: https://digitalcybersoft.github.io/scorchedearth-html5/ Nothing to install - it is a static HTML5 page that runs in the browser. It reproduces the original's turn-based tank artillery - destructible terrain, the weapon shop, the computer players, the physics and wind, the economy and scoring - reconstructed function-for-function and verified against the original's behavior. ## Screenshots Captured from this TypeScript / Canvas port running in the browser: | | | | |:---:|:---:|:---:| |
Title screen |
Player and tank setup |
A turn in progress | |
A shell detonates |
A direct hit |
The weapon shop | |
In-game control panel |
Round rankings |
Final scoring | ## Credit: Wendell Hicken Scorched Earth, subtitled "The Mother of All Games," was created by **Wendell Hicken** and distributed as shareware for DOS. The original is Copyright (c) 1991-1995 Wendell Hicken. All rights to Scorched Earth - its name, design, artwork, sound, terrain data, and original code - belong to him. His site is `whicken.com`. This project is an independent, **non-commercial tribute**. It is **not affiliated with, endorsed by, or supported by Wendell Hicken**. The game design is entirely his; this port only re-expresses its mechanics in TypeScript so the game can run in a browser today. If you want the genuine article, seek out Wendell Hicken's original. ## How it was built, and how faithful it is This is not a fresh interpretation - it is a *verified reimplementation*: 1. The original DOS binary was reverse-engineered **statically** (it is never executed) into a function-for-function **Python/pygame port** ([scorchedearth-python](https://github.com/DigitalCyberSoft/scorchedearth-python)), itself differential-tested against the recovered machine code. 2. This HTML5 build is a TypeScript rewrite of that Python port, with the Python port as the **oracle**: every module is proven to reproduce its Python counterpart. The verification: - **15,705 differential tests** (`npm test`, vitest) assert the TypeScript reproduces the Python port's output **exactly** (integers, pixels, bytes) or within a tight epsilon (transcendental math only). The RNG reproduces CPython's Mersenne Twister bit-for-bit; the game engine is checked by 29,814 turn/round state snapshots; the sprites by ~8M pixel assertions. - A **visual regression gate** (`visual/`, `bash visual/run_gate.sh`) renders identical seeded game states through both the TypeScript Canvas renderer and the Python pygame renderer and pixel-diffs them. The game **world** - sky, terrain, tanks - comes out **byte-identical** (zero channel delta). Only on-screen text differs, because a browser's font rasterizer is not pygame's; that is expected and reported separately. The original binary is never run by anything in this repository. ## Play Open **https://digitalcybersoft.github.io/scorchedearth-html5/** in any modern browser. There is nothing to install - it is a static HTML5 page (Canvas2D + Web Audio + JavaScript). A short loading bar fetches the assets, then the menu appears. Controls: Left/Right aim the turret, Up/Down adjust power, Tab cycles weapons, Space or Enter fires, number keys select a tank, F11 toggles fullscreen, Esc backs out. The menus, the weapon shop, and the in-game control panel (battery, parachute, shield) are mouse-driven. ## Building from source (developers only) The game is written in TypeScript and compiled **once** to the browser JavaScript that ships above; players never run any of this. It is only for modifying the code. ```bash npm install npm run dev # dev server at http://localhost:5173 npm run build # static bundle into dist/ (what GitHub Pages serves) npm test # the 15,705 differential tests against the Python oracle ``` ## The original assets This repository **includes** Wendell Hicken's original v1.5 data files under `public/assets/` - the 10 `.MTN` digitized mountains, `TALK1.CFG` / `TALK2.CFG` tank taunts, and `SCORCH.ICO` - so the game plays with the genuine landscapes and taunts out of the box. **These files are Wendell Hicken's property**, included only to keep this tribute faithful and immediately playable; they are not the authors' to license. The engine also runs without them (procedural terrain, gradient title, no taunts). ## How the code is organized | Module | Reverses | |--------|----------| | `rng.ts` | CPython Mersenne Twister, bit-exact (the determinism linchpin) | | `constants.ts` | byte-verified physics / damage / scoring / color-band constants | | `terrain.ts` | the pixel framebuffer, terrain generation, carve / deposit / settle | | `physics.ts` | the projectile integrator (gravity, wind, viscosity, speed clamp) | | `weapons.ts`, `weapon_behaviors.ts` | the 48-item table; rollers, diggers, MIRV, laser, riot | | `damage.ts`, `death.ts`, `hazard.ts` | radial damage, shields, fall damage, death throes, sky hazards | | `ai.ts`, `guidance.ts` | the seven computer types and the aiming oracle | | `economy.ts`, `scoring.ts` | the free-market shop, interest, scoring and rankings | | `game.ts` | the round / turn loop, fire / impact pipeline, win test | | `pygame.ts` | a faithful pygame API over Canvas2D (Surface, draw, surfarray, font) | | `render.ts`, `ui.ts`, `widgets.ts`, `screens.ts`, `ingame.ts` | rendering, HUD, menus, shop, dialogs | | `sprites.ts`, `palette.ts`, `sound.ts` | the recovered art + `.MTN` decoder, color tables, Web Audio | | `mtn.ts` | the `.MTN` terrain-photo decoder | | `main.ts` | the requestAnimationFrame loop, input, state machine, asset boot, IndexedDB saves | `oracle/` holds the Python vector dumpers; `test/` the differential suite; `visual/` the rendering gate. ## License and use The TypeScript, HTML, and CSS authored in this repository are the authors' own work and grant no rights to Scorched Earth itself. Game mechanics and rules, as distinct from a specific implementation, are generally understood not to be protected by copyright in the US; this port reimplements only the mechanics. Scorched Earth, its name, and all of its assets remain the property of Wendell Hicken. Please treat this as a personal, non-commercial tribute for play and study.

# Rayman (1995, MS-DOS) - matching decompilation

Goal: original DOS binaries -> verified matching C reconstruction -> source-complete game -> native SDL3 port ->
optional modernisation. The original executable is the authority; matching comes first.

Primary oracle: GOG `RAYMAN.EXE` **v1.21** (SHA-256 `599b1df2…09eb6`); secondary: CD/installed **v1.12**; PS1
`SLUS-000.05` as a semantic reference. See `docs/ORIGINALS.md`, `docs/VERSIONS.md`.

Status: 1,581 STRICT functions (63.4% of game code bytes), all original hand-written assembly STRICT, the complete
program links from source (not yet byte-identical). Numbers: `python tools/status.py`; details: `docs/STATUS.md`;
priorities: `docs/NEXT_STEPS.md`.

## Layout
| path | content |
|---|---|
| `assets/` | original files (user-supplied, ignored, read-only): `GOG/`, `DOS/`, `DOS_CD/`, `PS1/` |
| `external/` | read-only references: rayman-ps1-decomp, rayverse, rayman_disasm |
| `config/` | `oracles.json` (pinned originals), `toolchain.json` (pinned tools + profile), `symbols.json` (name -> address bindings), `units.json` (accepted units, zero-regression baseline) |
| `src/` | reconstructed game C units; each function's verified status is in `config/units.json` |
| `tools/` | extraction, analysis, compile and verification scripts (Python 3.10+, stdlib + capstone) |
| `tests/` | verifier self-tests (positive + negative controls) |
| `docs/` | findings and workflow |
| `build/`, `scratch/` | generated data, worker dirs, experiments (ignored) |

## Requirements
Python 3.10+ with `capstone` (5.0.x) and `pycparser` (permuter only); historical tools under `C:\tools` (override with `RAYMAN_TOOLS`), pinned in
`config/toolchain.json` and listed in `docs/TOOLCHAIN.md`: Watcom C/C++ 10.6 at `C:\tools\watcom-10.6` (required),
10.5/10.0/10.0a as controls.

## Commands (all verified working)
```
python tools/inventory.py --compare      # hash all assets incl. files inside the CD images; DOS install vs CD
python tools/extract.py --all            # PMW1 decode of both DOS oracles -> build/oracles/<id>/ (self-checks)
python tools/libscan.py C:/tools/watcom-10.6/LIB386/DOS/CLIB3R.LIB            # runtime members in the oracle
python tools/libscan.py --compare C:/tools/watcom-10.5/LIB386/DOS/CLIB3R.LIB C:/tools/watcom-10.6/LIB386/DOS/CLIB3R.LIB
python tools/libscan.py --symbols C:/tools/watcom-10.6/LIB386/DOS/CLIB3R.LIB C:/tools/watcom-10.6/LIB386/MATH387R.LIB
python tools/xref.py                     # DOS <-> Rayverse <-> PS1 table -> build/xref/xref.tsv ; `xref.py NAME` queries
python tools/tumap.py --list             # candidate original object boundaries with their functions
python tools/disasm.py myRand            # annotated disassembly (name, 1:off, ida:addr)
python tools/wcc.py --profile game src/rand.c -fo=build/rand.obj      # pinned, isolated compile
python tools/match.py src/rand.c         # compile + strict verify + first-difference report
python tools/verify.py                   # clean rebuild of all accepted units, zero-regression gate
python -m unittest discover -s tests     # verifier self-tests
python tools/status.py                   # progress derived from config/units.json + last verify report
python tools/promote.py OVERLAY.json [OLD=NEW]      # integrator: merge worker bindings (refuses conflicts/overlaps)
python tools/promote.py --unit NAME src/X.c         # integrator: register a unit with freshly measured statuses
python tools/seed.py draft 14e90 15e60      # seed an untouched object from PS1/Rayverse C into a draft unit (docs/SEEDING.md)
python tools/seed.py try NAME           # seed one function, compile in context, diagnose against the oracle
python tools/census.py && python tools/census.py --brief UNIT   # structural NEAR diagnosis + worker brief (docs/CENSUS.md)
python tools/explain.py UNIT FUNC         # why a NEAR function differs (allocator/scheduler mechanisms)
python tools/permute.py SRC.c FUNC --aggressive --seed 1 --max-compiles 800 --out build/permute/X   # source permuter
python -B tools/manifest.py && python -B tools/link.py all   # natural link of the whole program (build/link)
python tools/wpack.py verify             # one-off: unpack the Watcom 10.5 CD install set (provisioning, docs/TOOLCHAIN.md)
```
`--oracle dos_v112_us` selects the secondary oracle for `libscan`, `disasm`, `tumap`, `match`.
First-time order: `inventory` (optional) -> `extract --all` -> `libscan --symbols` (each oracle, with its libraries:
10.6 for v1.21, 10.5 for v1.12) -> `xref` -> `verify`.

## Rules
`AGENTS.md` (working rules), `docs/MATCHING.md` (workflow, status definitions), `docs/COMPILER.md` (evidence).

# Hocus Pocus Reconstruction

## Purpose

This repository is a place to make changes (fixes/additions) to Hocus Pocus (1994) but with source control. Most likely, the repository owner (Violet CLM) will make changes in a single branch for a few days, and then get bored and move on. But maybe there'll be pull requests and forks and all that community stuff! There's no way to know.

## Installation

On your computer, this repository must be in the same folder as a copy of the Hocus Pocus game, preferably the Registered 1.1. That is to say, `Hocus.dat` and `HocMake.bat` must be in the same folder, and `RECONSTR` must be a subfolder of that same folder.

## Compilation

Create a shortcut that runs `HocMake.bat` through your local copy of DOSBox, then run that shortcut. You can use the same shortcut for building and playing the game: HocMake.bat builds any files that have been changed since you last built the game, and then runs the game.

For example, your shortcut might be:
**Target:** `"C:\DOSBOX\DOSBox.exe" "C:\Games\DOS\HocusRec\HocMake.bat"`
**Start in:** `C:\Games\DOS\HocusRec\`

If you want to run the game with any command line options, either change the last line in HocMake.bat (e.g. `HOCUS -MENU` instead of just `HOCUS`), or else make yourself a separate shortcut that opens Hocus.exe directly.

## Context/Credits

This is [K1n9_Duk3](http://k1n9duk3.shikadi.net/)'s reconstruction of Hocus Pocus's source code as described/announced in [this PCKF thread](https://pckf.com/viewtopic.php?t=18675), but uploaded to github, and with the Borland C++ 3.1 compiler included for convenience.

K1n9_Duk3 recommends using Borland 2.0 for the Apogee Sound System code, and 3.1 for the game code, in order to compile the game as a byte-identical copy of the original releases. This repository intends to *make changes to* the original releases, so being able to produce a byte-identical copy is not considered important. The two `MOUNTDIR.BAT` files are edited to point to this Borland folder, and use relative paths, so that you may install this repository into any folder you wish.

Almost all code here, except as visible in the commit history, was the work of K1n9_Duk3. It continues to be released under the terms of the GNU GPL.
